statement: When the positive default correlation between a CDS reference entity and the protection seller increases, the CDS spread decreases, because joint default becomes more likely and the protection is less likely to pay out.
explanation: The buyer collects only if the reference entity defaults and the seller survives. Higher positive correlation raises the joint default probability while the reference entity's own default probability is unchanged, so the protection is worth less and the fair spread falls.
originalText: The spread decreases, because joint default of A and B becomes more likely and the protection is less likely to pay out.

statement: A higher positive default correlation between a CDS reference entity and the protection seller raises the CDS spread, because the reference entity becomes more likely to default.
explanation: Correlation does not change the reference entity's own default probability. It raises the chance that the seller also fails, which lowers the value of the protection and therefore the spread.
originalText: The spread increases, because A is more likely to default and the protection is therefore more valuable.

statement: A CDS spread depends only on the default probability of the reference entity and not on the default correlation between the reference entity and the protection seller.
explanation: The CDS spread depends on both the reference entity's default probability and the joint default correlation with the protection seller, because the buyer is exposed to the seller's default.
originalText: There is no effect, because the spread depends only on the default probability of the reference entity A.

statement: A higher positive default correlation between a CDS reference entity and the protection seller raises the CDS spread, because the protection seller must be compensated for its own greater default risk.
explanation: The seller's default risk is borne by the protection buyer, who therefore pays a lower spread, not a higher one, when the correlation rises.
originalText: The spread increases, because the protection seller B must be compensated for its own greater default risk.

statement: A positive correlation between two pricing factors indicates that when factor A rises in value, factor B is likely to rise in value as well.
explanation: Positive correlation means the two factors tend to move in the same direction. Correlation lies between -1 and +1 and measures direction and strength of co-movement, not a one-for-one change.
originalText: When factor A goes up in value, factor B is likely to rise in value.

statement: A positive correlation between two pricing factors indicates that when factor A rises in value, factor B is likely to fall in value.
explanation: That describes negative correlation. Positive correlation means the factors tend to move in the same direction.
originalText: When factor A goes up in value, factor B is likely to fall in value.
correction: A positive correlation between two pricing factors indicates that when factor A rises in value, factor B is likely to rise in value.

statement: A positive correlation between two pricing factors indicates that when factor A rises in value, factor B tends to be unaffected.
explanation: Factor B being unaffected describes zero correlation, that is, no linear relationship. Positive correlation means the factors tend to move together.
originalText: When factor A goes up in value, factor B tends to be unaffected.

statement: In May 2005, hedge funds long the CDO equity tranche and short the mezzanine tranche lost on both legs after the GM and Ford downgrades, because equity tranche spreads rose while mezzanine spreads fell and the tranches did not move together.
explanation: The funds assumed the two tranches would hedge each other, but misunderstood correlation across tranches. The equity spread rose and the mezzanine spread fell, so the long equity and the short mezzanine positions both lost.
originalText: Equity tranche spreads rose while mezzanine spreads fell, because the correlation properties across tranches were misunderstood and the tranches did not move together.

statement: After the GM and Ford downgrades in 2005, CDO equity tranche spreads fell and mezzanine tranche spreads rose.
explanation: The moves were the other way round: the equity tranche spread rose sharply while the mezzanine spread fell, because correlation fell for investment-grade CDOs.
originalText: Equity tranche spreads fell and mezzanine spreads rose, because default correlations across all tranches increased sharply.
correction: After the GM and Ford downgrades in 2005, CDO equity tranche spreads rose and mezzanine tranche spreads fell.

statement: Losses on CDO investments in the 2007-2009 crisis reflected that risk managers did not properly understand the correlation properties across CDO tranches, even though a copula model was trusted to monitor them.
explanation: The reading attributes the losses to misunderstood correlation across tranches in structured products, not to the CDO structure itself.
originalText: Risk managers did not properly understand the correlation properties across the CDO tranches, even though a copula model was trusted to monitor them.

statement: Default correlations among mortgages and across CDO tranches stayed low throughout the 2007-2009 crisis.
explanation: Default correlations rose sharply in 2007 together with default probabilities, which eroded the protection of senior tranches.
originalText: Default correlations among mortgages and across tranches stayed low throughout the crisis, so diversification failed only because default probabilities rose.
correction: Default correlations among mortgages and across CDO tranches rose sharply during the 2007-2009 crisis.

statement: Hedge funds holding long equity tranche and short mezzanine tranche positions were unaffected by correlation because the two positions fully offset each other.
explanation: The hedge failed precisely because both legs lost money when the tranche spreads moved against the funds, which led to hedge fund bankruptcies in 2005.
originalText: Hedge funds were unaffected by correlation because their long equity and short mezzanine positions fully offset each other.

statement: Ceteris paribus, an increase in the default correlation among the mortgages in a CDO increases the equity tranche spread.
explanation: The equity tranche is long correlation: higher default correlation lowers the equity tranche spread. In 2007 this effect was overshadowed by a dramatic rise in default probabilities.
originalText: Due to an increase in the default correlation among mortgages in collateralized debt obligations (CDOs), ceteris paribus, equity tranche spreads increased
correction: Ceteris paribus, an increase in the default correlation among the mortgages in a CDO decreases the equity tranche spread.

statement: The Gaussian copula correlation model was widely used to value CDOs, but trust in it was naive, for example because low default probabilities and low default correlations between CDO assets were often assumed as inputs.
explanation: The copula was trusted naively with low default probability and low correlation inputs, which understated the risk of the senior tranches.
originalText: The Gaussian copula correlation model was widely used to value collateralized debt obligations (CDOs), but the trust in the Gaussian copula was naive; for example, low default probabilities and default correlations (between CDO assets) were often assumed as model inputs

statement: Correlations between the tranches of CDOs increased during the crisis, and this had a devastating effect on the super-senior tranches.
explanation: Rising correlation across tranches in 2007 eroded the protection that the super-senior tranches were assumed to enjoy.
originalText: Correlations between the tranches of the CDOs increased during the crisis, and this had a devastating effect on the super‑senior tranches

statement: Credit default swaps were used as speculative instruments in ways that did not disperse risk as insurance contracts are expected to disperse risk.
explanation: CDS sellers such as AIG concentrated rather than dispersed risk, so the risk transfer did not work as insurance would.
originalText: Credit default swaps (CDS) were used as speculative instruments in ways that did not disperse risk like we expect insurance contracts to disperse risk

statement: A protection seller on the most senior CDO tranche gains value when the default correlation among the underlying assets falls, because the likelihood that the protection is triggered diminishes.
explanation: The senior tranche is short correlation: it is hit only by widespread simultaneous default, which is less likely when correlation is lower. The protection seller therefore gains.
originalText: The value of the position will significantly increase, as the likelihood of activating the credit protection diminishes.

statement: The value of a position in a senior CDO tranche is unaffected by changes in default correlation, since only expected default losses matter.
explanation: Correlation leaves total expected portfolio loss unchanged but redistributes it across tranches, so the value of a single tranche does change.
originalText: The position’s value will remain unaffected, since only the expected default losses are relevant, and default correlation does not influence these losses.

statement: A protection seller on the most senior CDO tranche loses value when the default correlation among the underlying assets rises sharply, because the probability that the protection must be paid increases.
explanation: Senior tranches are short correlation: higher correlation raises the probability of mass simultaneous default reaching the senior tranche, so the premium received becomes too low for the risk.
originalText: It will lose significant value, since the probability of exercising the protection increases.

statement: A protection seller on the most senior CDO tranche gains value when the default correlation among the underlying assets rises, because the probability that the protection must be paid falls.
explanation: With rising correlation the chance of a payout on the senior tranche increases, so the protection seller loses value. The gain described applies when correlation falls.
originalText: It will gain significant value because the probability of exercising the protection falls.
correction: A protection seller on the most senior CDO tranche loses value when the default correlation among the underlying assets rises, because the probability that the protection must be paid rises.

statement: CDS risk was concentrated in an overextended seller such as AIG rather than dispersed as insurance would suggest, so rising defaults and correlation produced payouts the seller could not meet.
explanation: CDS are meant to transfer and spread default risk, but concentration in thinly capitalised sellers meant the crisis losses could not be absorbed.
originalText: CDS risk was concentrated in an overextended seller rather than dispersed as insurance would suggest, so rising defaults and correlation produced payouts the seller could not meet.

statement: AIG had bought, rather than sold, most of its CDS protection, so the failure of its counterparties left it unhedged.
explanation: AIG was a net seller of protection, with about USD 500 billion sold and little reinsurance. The problem was its sold positions.
originalText: AIG had bought, not sold, most of the protection, so the failure of its counterparties left it unhedged.

statement: The CDS market shrank sharply between 2004 and 2007, removing institutions' ability to hedge default risk.
explanation: The CDS market grew from about USD 8 trillion to about USD 60 trillion over 2004-2007.
originalText: The CDS market shrank during 2004‑2007, removing the ability of institutions to hedge default risk.

statement: Protection sellers in the CDS market made large gains as default correlation increased.
explanation: Protection sellers lose when defaults and default correlation rise, as AIG did.
originalText: CDS values rose as default correlation increased, so protection sellers made large gains that distorted markets.

statement: Holding default probability constant, an increase in default correlations between mortgages in a CDO typically lowers the equity tranche spread.
explanation: Higher default correlation concentrates defaults in the same scenarios, making it less likely that the equity tranche is hit alone, so its spread falls.

statement: Because stochastic correlation is non-deterministic, stochastic correlation models should be avoided.
explanation: Stochastic correlation processes are a main approach to modelling correlation. Non-determinism is the point of the approach, not a reason to avoid it.
originalText: Because stochastic correlation is non‑deterministic, stochastic correlation models should be avoided.

statement: Correlation risk is less important in market risk and credit risk but more important in operational risk.
explanation: Correlation is central to market risk, through the covariance matrix in VaR and expected shortfall, and to credit risk, through default correlation.

statement: A 99% VaR over a 10-day horizon is exceeded in only one of every hundred 10-day periods.
explanation: 99% VaR is a loss threshold that is exceeded in only 1% of periods of the stated horizon.
originalText: Only once in a hundred 10‑day periods will losses exceed this VaR amount (\$1.7486 million).

statement: A 99% VaR means we are 99% confident that we can lose more than the VaR amount over the horizon.
explanation: A 99% VaR means we are 99% confident that losses over the horizon will not exceed the VaR amount.
originalText: We are 99% confident that we can lose more than \$1.7486 million of our two‑asset portfolio in the next 10 days.
correction: A 99% VaR means we are 99% confident that we will not lose more than the VaR amount over the horizon.

statement: A 99% VaR over a 10-day horizon is exceeded only once every 10,000 days.
explanation: A 99% 10-day VaR is exceeded in 1 of 100 ten-day periods, which is about once every 1,000 trading days, not 10,000.
originalText: Only once every 10,000 days will this VaR amount (\$1.7486 million) be exceeded.
correction: A 99% VaR over a 10-day horizon is exceeded only once every 1,000 days.

statement: When two assets are perfectly correlated, portfolio VaR equals the sum of the two stand-alone VaRs.
explanation: At $\rho = 1$ the square root in the VaR formula collapses to $\text{VaR}_1 + \text{VaR}_2$, so there is no diversification benefit.
originalText: When the assets are perfectly correlated, expression II is correct.

statement: When two assets are perfectly correlated, portfolio VaR is strictly less than the sum of the two stand-alone VaRs.
explanation: A strict inequality holds only when $\rho < 1$. At perfect correlation there is no diversification benefit and portfolio VaR equals the sum.
originalText: When the assets are perfectly correlated, expression I is correct.
correction: When two assets are perfectly correlated, portfolio VaR is equal to the sum of the two stand-alone VaRs.

statement: Under the variance-covariance method, portfolio VaR equals the simple sum of the individual position VaRs only when the returns of the positions are perfectly positively correlated.
explanation: At $\rho = 1$ the cross term is at its maximum and the VaR formula collapses to the sum. Any $\rho < 1$ gives a portfolio VaR strictly below the sum.
originalText: Perfectly positively correlated

statement: Under the variance-covariance method, portfolio VaR equals the simple sum of the individual position VaRs when the returns of the positions are positively correlated with a correlation coefficient below 1.
explanation: Positive correlation below 1 still leaves portfolio VaR strictly below the sum of the individual VaRs. Only perfect positive correlation removes all diversification.
originalText: Positively correlated, with a correlation coefficient below 1
correction: Under the variance-covariance method, portfolio VaR equals the simple sum of the individual position VaRs when the returns of the positions are perfectly positively correlated.

changes.from: positively correlated with a correlation coefficient below 1

statement: Under the variance-covariance method, portfolio VaR equals the simple sum of the individual position VaRs when the returns of the positions are perfectly negatively correlated.
explanation: At $\rho = -1$ portfolio VaR is the absolute difference of the VaRs, its minimum possible value. The sum is reached at $\rho = 1$.
originalText: Perfectly negatively correlated
correction: Under the variance-covariance method, portfolio VaR equals the simple sum of the individual position VaRs when the returns of the positions are perfectly positively correlated.

statement: Portfolio VaR is maximised when the pairwise correlations between the returns of the underlying assets are perfectly positive.
explanation: VaR rises with correlation through the cross term and is capped at the sum of the stand-alone VaRs when $\rho = 1$.
originalText: Perfectly positive

statement: Portfolio VaR is maximised when the pairwise correlations between the returns of the underlying assets are perfectly negative.
explanation: Perfect negative correlation gives the minimum portfolio VaR, not the maximum. The maximum occurs at perfect positive correlation.
originalText: Perfectly negative
correction: Portfolio VaR is maximised when the pairwise correlations between the returns of the underlying assets are perfectly positive.

statement: Expected shortfall measures market risk for extreme events, typically for the worst 0.1%, 1% or 5% of possible future scenarios.
explanation: Expected shortfall characterises tail risk: it is the average loss beyond the VaR cutoff, at typical confidence levels of 99.9%, 99% and 95%.
originalText: It measures market risk for extreme events, typically for the worst 0.1%, 1%, or 5% of possible future scenarios.

statement: Intersector default correlations are typically lower than intrasector default correlations, so lenders should create a sector-diversified loan portfolio.
explanation: Defaults are more correlated within an industry than across industries, so spreading loans across sectors lowers default correlation and joint-loss risk.
originalText: Intersector default correlations are typically lower than intrasector default correlations, so lenders should create a sector‑diversified loan portfolio.

statement: Intersector default correlations are typically higher than intrasector default correlations.
explanation: Default correlations are higher within a sector than across sectors, because systematic sector factors dominate.
originalText: Intersector default correlations are typically higher than intrasector default correlations, so lenders should create a sector‑diversified loan portfolio.
correction: Intersector default correlations are typically lower than intrasector default correlations.

statement: Intrasector default correlations are typically higher than intersector default correlations, so lenders should specialise in a single-sector loan portfolio.
explanation: The relationship is right but the conclusion is wrong: a single-sector book concentrates highly correlated exposures. Lenders should diversify across sectors.
originalText: Intrasector default correlations are typically higher than intersector default correlations, so lenders should specialize in a single‑sector loan portfolio.

statement: Portfolio diversification based on correlations estimated over a period without a crisis will most likely fail in a major economic crisis and lead to losses, because correlations rise sharply in a crisis.
explanation: Correlations are not stable and spike in systemic crises, for example US equity correlations rose from about 27% to over 50% in 2008-09. Diversification benefits disappear when they are needed.
originalText: Portfolio diversification would most likely fail and lead to losses.

statement: Well-diversified portfolios are not affected by a major economic crisis.
explanation: Diversification does not protect in all states, because correlations rise in a crisis and assets fall together.
originalText: The fund managers would not be affected as their portfolios are well diversified.

statement: The probability of default is higher in the long-term time horizon for non-investment-grade bonds.
explanation: Distressed issuers face their highest default risk in the near term. The default term structure of non-investment-grade bonds slopes downward.
originalText: The probability of default is higher in the long‑term time horizon for non‑investment‑grade bonds.
correction: The probability of default is higher in the short-term time horizon for non-investment-grade bonds.

statement: Creditors benefit by diversifying exposure across industries to lower the default correlations of debtors.
explanation: Default correlations are higher within industries than across them, so cross-industry diversification lowers default correlation.

statement: The default term structure increases with time to maturity for most investment-grade bonds.
explanation: Investment-grade issuers have more time to suffer adverse changes, so the cumulative default probability rises with maturity.
originalText: The default term structure increases with time to maturity for most investment‑grade bonds.

statement: Equity correlations estimated from a period of continuous economic expansion will understate the correlations that prevail in a recession, so the diversification benefit in stress is overstated.
explanation: Average equity correlation is lowest in expansions (about 27.5%) and highest in recessions (about 37.0%). A sample with no recession therefore gives estimates below stressed levels.
originalText: The estimated correlations will understate the correlations that prevail in a recession, so the diversification benefit in stress is overstated.

statement: Equity correlations estimated from a period of continuous economic expansion will overstate the correlations that prevail in a recession, so the diversification benefit in stress is understated.
explanation: Expansion correlations are the lowest, not the highest, so an expansion-only sample understates recession correlations and overstates diversification in stress.
originalText: The estimated correlations will overstate the correlations that prevail in a recession, so the diversification benefit in stress is understated.
correction: Equity correlations estimated from a period of continuous economic expansion will understate the correlations that prevail in a recession, so the diversification benefit in stress is overstated.

statement: Equity correlations are independent of the state of the economy, so the choice of estimation window does not matter.
explanation: Equity correlations are state dependent: about 27.5% in expansions against about 37.0% in recessions, so the window matters.
originalText: Equity correlations are independent of the state of the economy, so the choice of window does not matter.

statement: The autocorrelation of equity correlations is a monotonically increasing function of the monthly lag, so higher lags imply higher autocorrelations.
explanation: Autocorrelation of equity correlations decays as the lag lengthens, from about 22% at one month to about 10% at ten months.
originalText: Autocorrelation is a monotonically increasing function of the monthly lag; higher lags imply higher autocorrelations.
correction: The autocorrelation of equity correlations is a monotonically decreasing function of the monthly lag, so higher lags imply lower autocorrelations.

statement: Mean reversion should be included in equity correlation models.
explanation: Equity correlations show strong mean reversion, at a rate of about 78%, so a model of them should include it.

statement: For equity correlations, the Johnson SB distribution fits better than the normal or lognormal distribution.
explanation: The bounded and flexible Johnson SB distribution was the best fit for equity correlations.
originalText: For equity correlations, the Johnson SB distribution is better than the normal or lognormal.

statement: Equity correlations are highest in recessions, while equity correlation volatility is highest in normal periods.
explanation: Average correlation is 37.0% in recessions, 33.0% in normal periods and 27.5% in expansions, while correlation volatility is 83.0% in normal periods, 80.5% in recessions and 71.2% in expansions.
originalText: correlations are highest for recessions, and correlation volatility is highest for normal periods.

statement: Equity correlations and equity correlation volatility are both highest in recessions.
explanation: Correlation level peaks in recessions, but correlation volatility peaks in normal periods (about 83.0%) rather than recessions (about 80.5%).
originalText: correlations and correlation volatility are highest for recessions.

statement: Flexible copula functions became popular around 2000 because they offered a simple way to correlate many assets, such as 100 or more in a CDO, with a single multidimensional function, but they fell out of favour when the 2007-2009 financial crisis began.
explanation: Copulas were attractive for solving a complex correlation problem with simple methods, and their reputation suffered in the 2007-2009 crisis.
originalText: They offered a simple way to correlate many assets (e.g., 100+ assets in a CDO) with a single multidimensional function, but fell out of favor when the 2007–2009 financial crisis began.

statement: Copula functions fell out of favour because they could only be applied when the marginal distributions were normal.
explanation: A key advantage of a copula is that the marginals can have any shape, because they are mapped to a known distribution. Normal marginals are not required.
originalText: They removed the need to specify marginal distributions, but fell out of favor because they could only be applied when the marginals were normal.

statement: Copula functions allow default correlation to be estimated without any assumptions.
explanation: Copulas still require assumptions, for example about the form of the copula and its correlation input.
originalText: They allowed default correlation to be estimated without any assumptions, but fell out of favor after the 1998 collapse of Long‑Term Capital Management.

statement: A copula function specifies a single multivariate distribution as a function of various, even unusual, univariate marginal distributions by mapping them to distributions with an accessible form.
explanation: A copula joins separate marginals of any shape into one joint distribution by mapping each to a well-behaved distribution such as the standard normal, where a correlation structure is easy to define.
originalText: To specify a single multivariate distribution as a function of various (even unusual) univariate marginal distributions, by mapping them to distributions with an accessible form.

statement: The purpose of a copula function is to decompose a posterior conditional distribution into a combination of the prior probability, the likelihood and the marginal probability.
explanation: That describes Bayes' theorem. A copula joins univariate marginal distributions into a multivariate distribution.
originalText: To decompose a posterior conditional distribution into a combination of the prior probability, the likelihood, and the marginal probability.

statement: A copula function joins n univariate distributions into one multivariate, n-dimensional distribution.
explanation: A copula maps n marginal distributions onto a known distribution and joins them, keeping the original marginals and adding a dependence structure.
originalText: A copula function joins (n) univariate distributions to one multivariate (n‑dimensional) distribution.

statement: A copula correlates a stock price and its volatility, which allows it to model the equity-implied volatility skew.
explanation: Correlating a price with its volatility describes a stochastic volatility model. A copula joins univariate marginal distributions into a multivariate distribution.
originalText: A copula correlates a stock price (S) and its volatility (σ) which allows it to model equity‑implied volatility skew.

statement: A copula function is a limiting special case of the Pearson model and analyses only the linear relationship between variables.
explanation: A copula is not a special case of the Pearson model and is not limited to linear relationships. It is used precisely because Pearson correlation is limited.
originalText: A copula function is a limiting (special) case of the Pearson model, such that it only analyzes the linear relationship between variables.

statement: A copula maps each marginal distribution, percentile to percentile, to a known distribution such as the standard normal, defines a correlation between the mapped variables, and so obtains a joint distribution that preserves the original marginals.
explanation: Correlation cannot be directly and sensibly defined between skewed or heavy-tailed marginals. Mapping them to the standard normal makes it possible, and because the mapping is invertible each original marginal is preserved.
originalText: Map each empirical marginal percentile‑to‑percentile to the standard normal distribution, define a correlation between the mapped variables, and thereby obtain a joint distribution that preserves both original marginals.

statement: All major copula functions natively ensure that a linear Pearson correlation input accurately describes the actual dependence structure, even if the dependence is dynamic.
explanation: A copula adds flexibility on the marginals, but its dependence parameter is only as good as the correlation input. Pearson correlation measures only linear dependence, and a copula does not guarantee a correct or dynamic dependence structure.
originalText: She used the linear Pearson correlation coefficient as an input to the copulas, and all major copula functions will natively ensure this parameter accurately describes the actual dependence structure, even if the dependence is dynamic.

statement: A copula approach enables simulation of the entire distribution of loss outcomes, not only the tails.
explanation: A copula yields a full joint distribution that can be simulated across all outcomes.
originalText: The copula approach will enable her to simulate the entire distribution (i.e., in addition to the tails) of loss outcomes.

statement: Given the same set of univariate marginal distributions, one can test, by simulation, various one-factor or two-factor copula functions.
explanation: The marginals are fixed inputs, so alternative copulas can be run on the same marginals.
originalText: Given the same set of univariate marginal distributions, she will be able to test (i.e., simulate) with various one‑or two‑factor copula functions.

statement: Copula functions place no requirements on the univariate distributions they join, so skewed or heavy-tailed marginal distributions can be accommodated.
explanation: Each marginal is mapped to a known distribution, so the marginals can have any shape.
originalText: Several of the univariate loss distributions are skewed and/or heavy‑tailed, but copula functions are flexible to this non‑normal variety, as copulas place no requirements on the univariate distributions that are joined.

statement: Gaussian copulas are often used to quantify the default correlation structure underlying structured credit products.
explanation: The Gaussian copula is the standard and most widely applied copula in finance, notably for the default correlation structure of CDOs and other structured credit products.

statement: A copula maps a single univariate distribution to multiple multivariate distributions.
explanation: The direction is reversed: a copula maps several univariate distributions into one multivariate distribution.
correction: A copula maps multiple univariate distributions to a single multivariate distribution.

changes.from: a single univariate distribution to multiple multivariate distributions
changes.to: multiple univariate distributions to a single multivariate distribution

statement: Fréchet copulas incorporate a single factor and have historically been the most widely applied copulas in the finance industry.
explanation: The Gaussian copula, not the Fréchet copula, has been the most widely applied in finance, and Fréchet copulas are not single-factor copulas.

statement: A copula maps arbitrary marginal distributions, percentile to percentile, onto a well-behaved joint distribution such as the multivariate standard normal, and the correlation matrix of that joint distribution supplies the correlation structure.
explanation: A copula links marginals of unknown shape to a well-defined joint distribution by percentile mapping, using the correlation matrix as the dependence structure while preserving each marginal.
originalText: The marginals are mapped, percentile to percentile, to a well‑behaved joint distribution $F_{n}$ (such as the multivariate standard normal), and $\rho_{F}$ supplies the correlation structure between them.

statement: The marginal distributions joined by a copula must themselves be standard normal distributions for the copula to be defined.
explanation: The point of a copula is that the marginals can have any, even unknown, shape. Only the target distribution they are mapped to, such as the standard normal, is normal.
originalText: The marginals $G_{i}(u_{i})$ must themselves be standard normal distributions for the copula to be defined.

statement: Applying a copula changes each variable's marginal distribution so that it takes on the shape of the joint distribution it is mapped to.
explanation: The marginals are preserved. The mapping to a known distribution is used only to define the correlation structure.
originalText: Applying the copula changes each variable’s marginal distribution so that it takes on the shape of $F_{n}$.

statement: To simulate the default time of an asset under the Gaussian default time copula, a Cholesky decomposition of the correlation matrix is used to draw a correlated sample from the multivariate standard normal distribution, which is equated to the asset's cumulative default probability and solved for the default time, repeated over many samples.
explanation: The correlated sample $M_n(\bullet)$ is set equal to $Q_i(\tau)$ and solved for $\tau$. There is no closed form, so the process is repeated by simulation.
originalText: Use a Cholesky decomposition of the correlation matrix to draw a correlated sample $M_{n}(\bullet)$ from the n‑variate standard normal distribution (a value in \[0,1\]), equate it to the cumulative default probability $Q_{i}(\tau)$, solve for $\tau$, and repeat over many samples.

statement: Under the Gaussian default time copula, default times can be computed analytically in closed form from the average pairwise correlation, without simulation.
explanation: There is no closed-form solution, and an average correlation does not preserve the full correlation matrix, so random sampling is required.
originalText: Compute the expected default time analytically in closed form by solving $Q_{i}(\tau) = M_{n}(\bullet)$ once, using the average pairwise correlation.

statement: In the Gaussian default time copula, the default dependence between assets is supplied by the correlation matrix of the n-variate standard normal distribution.
explanation: Each cumulative default probability is mapped to a standard normal and fixes only that asset's marginal. The joint dependence is introduced solely through the correlation matrix.
originalText: The correlation matrix $\rho_{M}$ of the n‑variate standard normal distribution, containing the default correlations of asset i with all n assets.

statement: In the Gaussian default time copula, the cumulative default probabilities supply the default dependence between assets, because higher default probabilities imply higher default correlation.
explanation: The cumulative default probabilities are the marginal inputs that set each asset's individual default probability. The dependence comes from the correlation matrix.
originalText: The vector of cumulative default probabilities $Q_{i}(t)$, because higher default probabilities imply higher default correlation.

statement: In a Gaussian default time copula simulation of many assets, the correlated sample from the multivariate normal distribution is found through a Cholesky decomposition of the correlation matrix.
explanation: The Cholesky decomposition factors the correlation matrix so that independent normal draws can be transformed into correlated ones, which are then mapped to default times.
originalText: The Cholesky decomposition

statement: In a Gaussian copula simulation, a company defaults within a given period if its correlated normal draw is below the inverse cumulative normal value of its cumulative default probability for that period.
explanation: The cumulative default probability is transformed to a normal threshold, for example $N^{-1}(1\%) \approx -2.33$, and compared with a correlated normal draw, so default correlation is reflected.
originalText: Simulate a value from a multivariate normal distribution for each company. If the value is less than the inverse cumulative normal distribution value at 1% (‑2.33), default occurs within the first year.

statement: In regression-based hedging, the level regression regresses the yield of one bond on the yield of the other, whereas the change regression regresses changes in yield on changes in yield.
explanation: The level regression is $y_t = \alpha + \beta x_t + \epsilon_t$ using yield levels; the change regression is $\Delta y_t = \beta \Delta x_t + \Delta\epsilon_t$ using first differences.
originalText: It regresses $y_{t}$ on $x_{t}$ (yield on yield), whereas the change regression regresses $\Delta y_{t}$ on $\Delta x_{t}$.

statement: In regression-based hedging, the level regression produces biased coefficient estimates, whereas the change regression produces unbiased estimates.
explanation: Both approaches give unbiased and consistent coefficient estimates. The issue is efficiency, because the error terms are likely serially correlated.
originalText: It produces biased coefficient estimates, whereas the change regression produces unbiased estimates.

statement: In regression-based hedging, both the level and the change regression give unbiased and consistent coefficient estimates, but their error terms are likely serially correlated, so the estimates are not efficient.
explanation: Serial correlation in the errors leaves OLS unbiased and consistent but inefficient, in both specifications.
originalText: Both approaches give unbiased and consistent coefficient estimates, but their error terms are likely serially correlated, so the estimates are not efficient.

statement: In regression-based hedging, both the level and the change regression give efficient estimates because their error terms are independent over time.
explanation: Independent errors are the classical assumption, not the empirical finding. The errors are likely serially correlated, so the estimates are not efficient.
originalText: Both approaches give efficient estimates because the errors are independent over time.

statement: In regression-based hedging, the change regression gives biased estimates, while the level regression gives unbiased estimates.
explanation: Neither specification is biased. Both give unbiased and consistent estimates that are inefficient when the errors are serially correlated.
originalText: The change regression gives biased estimates, while the level regression gives unbiased estimates.

statement: The problem created by serial correlation in regression hedges cannot be overcome, so one of the two approaches must be selected and some methodological imperfection is inevitable.
explanation: A third approach, a level regression with autoregressive errors $\epsilon_t = \rho\epsilon_{t-1} + v_t$, handles the serial correlation, so the imperfection is not unavoidable.
originalText: The problem created by serial correlation cannot be overcome, and one of the two approaches must be selected, as some methodological imperfection is inevitable

statement: If the error terms are independently and identically distributed with mean zero and uncorrelated with the independent variable, the regression coefficient estimators are unbiased, consistent and efficient.
explanation: These are the classical regression conditions.
originalText: If the error terms are independently and identically distributed with mean zero and uncorrelated with the independent variable, then the regression coefficient estimators are unbiased, consistent, and efficient

statement: If the error terms are serially correlated, the regression coefficients will not be efficient, although they likely remain unbiased and consistent.
explanation: Serial correlation costs efficiency only, not unbiasedness or consistency.
originalText: If the error terms are serially correlated, the regression coefficients will not be efficient, although they likely remain unbiased and consistent

statement: In both the yield-on-yield and the change-on-change regression approaches, the error terms are completely uncorrelated.
explanation: Error terms are likely to be correlated over time in both approaches, so the OLS estimates are unbiased and consistent but not efficient.
originalText: In both cases, the error terms are completely uncorrelated.
correction: In both the yield-on-yield and the change-on-change regression approaches, the error terms are correlated over time.

statement: A regression hedge regresses the yield change of the bond being hedged on the yield change of the hedging instrument and uses the slope as the risk weight, whereas a reverse regression swaps the variables and gives a different hedge amount unless the fit is perfect.
explanation: The two regressions have different dependent variables and hence different slopes. They are reciprocals only when $R^2 = 1$.
originalText: A regression hedge regresses the corporate bond’s yield change on the Treasury’s yield change and sets the risk weight at that slope; a reverse regression regresses the Treasury’s yield change on the corporate bond’s, giving a different hedge amount unless the fit is perfect.

statement: A regression hedge regresses the yield change of the hedging instrument on the yield change of the bond being hedged, while a reverse regression does the opposite.
explanation: The regression hedge regresses the yield change of the hedged bond on that of the hedging instrument. The reverse regression swaps the roles.
originalText: A regression hedge regresses the yield change of the Treasury on the yield change of the corporate bond, while a reverse regression does the opposite.

statement: A regression hedge and a reverse-regression hedge give the same hedge amount, because the slope of the reverse regression is always the reciprocal of the original slope.
explanation: The slopes are reciprocals only when $R^2 = 1$. With an imperfect fit their product is $R^2$, not 1, so the hedge amounts differ.
originalText: Both approaches give the same hedge amount, because the reverse‑regression slope is always the reciprocal of the original slope.

statement: Reversing the dependent and independent variables changes the OLS slope from $\rho\sigma_Y/\sigma_X$ to $\rho\sigma_X/\sigma_Y$, and these slopes are not reciprocals unless $\rho = \pm 1$.
explanation: The product of the two slopes is $\rho^2$, so they are reciprocals only when the correlation is perfect. This is why regression and reverse-regression hedges differ.
originalText: Reversing the dependent and independent variables changes the OLS slope from $\rho\sigma_{Y}/\sigma_{X}$ to $\rho\sigma_{X}/\sigma_{Y}$, and these are not reciprocals unless $|\rho| = 1$.

statement: A regression and its reverse regression produce the same slope, because the correlation between the two series does not depend on direction.
explanation: Correlation is symmetric, but the slope also depends on the ratio of volatilities, which inverts when the variables are swapped.
originalText: Both regressions produce the same slope because the correlation between the two series does not depend on direction.

statement: In a binomial interest rate tree, the branch with the higher rate at the next date is called the up-state and the branch with the lower rate the down-state.
explanation: This is the standard terminology of the binomial tree.
originalText: Up‑state

statement: In a binomial interest rate tree, the value at a node is the average of the present values of the two possible values from the next period.
explanation: The two next-period values, including any coupon, are discounted at the node's one-period rate and weighted by their probabilities, 50% each in the standard tree.
originalText: average of the present values of the two possible values from the next period.

statement: In a binomial interest rate tree, the value at a node is the sum of the present values of the two possible values from the next period.
explanation: Summing would double-count the cash flow. The probabilities of one half must be applied, which gives the average of the two present values.
originalText: sum of the present values of the two possible values from the next period.
correction: In a binomial interest rate tree, the value at a node is the average of the present values of the two possible values from the next period.

statement: In arbitrage pricing of an interest rate derivative, the replicating portfolio must duplicate the derivative's cash flows in every possible interest rate scenario.
explanation: The derivative's payoff depends on the future rate, so matching it in every rate state forces the replica and the derivative to have the same price by no-arbitrage.
originalText: interest rate scenario

statement: In arbitrage pricing of an option by replication in a binomial tree, the real-world probabilities of up and down moves play no role in the option's price.
explanation: The replica's composition and cost are fixed by the state payoffs and market prices alone, so the true probabilities never enter the arbitrage price.
originalText: None; the arbitrage price does not depend on them

statement: In replicating an option in a binomial tree, the real-world probabilities of an up and a down move determine the number of units of the underlying bond in the replicating portfolio.
explanation: The number of units is a ratio of payoff differences to price differences across the two states, and involves no probabilities.
originalText: They determine the number of units of the underlying bond in the replicating portfolio

statement: In the risk-neutral world, the expected return on all assets is zero.
explanation: In the risk-neutral world all assets earn the risk-free short rate in expectation, not zero.
originalText: The replicating portfolio demonstrates that the expected return on all assets in the risk‑neutral world is zero
correction: In the risk-neutral world, the expected return on all assets equals the risk-free rate.

statement: The expected discounted value of a bond computed with the risk-neutral probabilities returns the bond's market price.
explanation: The risk-neutral probabilities are chosen so that the expected discounted value of the underlying securities reproduces their market prices.
originalText: The expected discounted value (EDV) of the bond using the risk‑neutral probabilities returns the bond’s market price of \$959.76

statement: Securities whose prices are derived by constructing a replicating portfolio of the underlying securities are called contingent claims and are priced by arbitrage arguments.
explanation: Underlying securities such as zero-coupon bonds have market prices taken as given. Securities whose payoffs depend on them, such as options on bonds, are contingent claims priced by no-arbitrage replication.
originalText: contingent claims, priced by arbitrage arguments

statement: Contingent claims are priced by their real-world expected discounted value.
explanation: Contingent claims are priced by arbitrage replication or, equivalently, by risk-neutral expected discounted value. Real-world probabilities ignore the replication argument.
originalText: contingent claims, priced by their real‑world expected discounted value

statement: Risk-neutral pricing is an efficient way to price many contingent claims under the same assumed interest rate process because the original process has to be modified only once.
explanation: The risk-neutral probabilities are calibrated once to the market prices of the underlying securities. Afterwards any claim on the same process is priced as its expected discounted value.
originalText: the original interest rate process has to be modified only once, and this modification only requires pricing the contingent claim(s) by arbitrage.

statement: Risk-neutral pricing is an efficient way to price many contingent claims because the original interest rate process does not need to be modified.
explanation: The true probabilities must be changed to risk-neutral ones once, by calibrating to market prices. Without that change, expected discounted values would not equal arbitrage prices.
originalText: the original interest rate process does not need to be modified, and there is no need to price the contingent claim(s) by arbitrage.

statement: The risk penalty implicit in the price of a call option on a zero-coupon bond priced by arbitrage is inherited from the premise that the market price of the zero is less than its expected discounted value.
explanation: Risk-averse investors price the zero below its expected discounted value under true probabilities. Arbitrage transmits that penalty to the option.
originalText: less than its expected discounted value.

statement: The risk penalty implicit in the price of a call option on a zero-coupon bond priced by arbitrage is inherited from the premise that the market price of the zero is greater than its expected discounted value.
explanation: The sign is reversed: risk aversion pushes the market price below the expected discounted value.
originalText: greater than its expected discounted value.
correction: The risk penalty implicit in the price of a call option on a zero-coupon bond priced by arbitrage is inherited from the premise that the market price of the zero is less than its expected discounted value.

statement: The arbitrage-free price of an option equals its expected discounted value under the risk-neutral probabilities.
explanation: Arbitrage forces the option price to equal its risk-neutral expected discounted value, in both the real and the imaginary economy.
originalText: The arbitrage‑free price of the option equals its expected discounted value under the risk‑neutral probabilities.

statement: The price of a security that is priced by arbitrage depends on investors' risk preferences.
explanation: Arbitrage prices are independent of risk preferences, which is why risk-neutral pricing works.
originalText: The price of a security that is priced by arbitrage depends on investors’ risk preferences.

statement: The price of an option does not necessarily need to be the same in the real and the imaginary risk-neutral economies.
explanation: The two economies are constructed to give identical prices for the underlying securities, and hence for any derivative priced by arbitrage.
originalText: The price of an option does not necessarily need to be the same in the real and imaginary economies.

statement: Risk-neutral pricing uses risk-neutral probabilities as inputs into an expected discounted value.
explanation: The expected-discounted-value form is kept, but the true probabilities are replaced with risk-neutral ones, so the risk penalty is carried by the probabilities while discounting uses the risk-free rate.
originalText: Risk‑neutral probabilities as inputs into expected discounted value

statement: In risk-neutral pricing, risk-neutral probabilities replace the risk-free rate in order to incorporate risk aversion.
explanation: Probabilities do not replace the rate. Discounting stays at the risk-free rate and the risk penalty is absorbed in the probabilities.
originalText: Risk‑neutral probabilities replace the risk‑free rate to incorporate risk aversion

statement: For risk-neutral pricing of contingent claims to be valid, the real-world expected return on the underlying security must equal the risk-free rate.
explanation: Replication makes the real-world expected return irrelevant. The underlying earns the risk-free rate only under the risk-neutral probabilities.
originalText: The real‑world expected return on the underlying security must equal the risk‑free rate for the method to be valid.

statement: In risk-neutral pricing of contingent claims, the risk-free rate is the appropriate discount rate.
explanation: After moving to risk-neutral probabilities, the risk penalty is in the probabilities and the risk-free rate is the correct discount rate.
originalText: The risk‑free rate is the appropriate discount rate.

statement: A derivative's price is the same in the imaginary risk-neutral world and in the real world.
explanation: The imaginary economy is built to match the market prices of the underlying securities, so the arbitrage price of the derivative coincides in both worlds.
originalText: The derivative’s price is the same in the imaginary (risk‑neutral) world and in the real world.

statement: The argument that contingent claims can be valued with risk-neutral pricing rests on the no-arbitrage price being invariant to investor risk preferences.
explanation: Replication hedges away the risky factor, so the no-arbitrage price does not depend on how risk-averse any investor is. Pricing in a risk-neutral world therefore gives the same answer.
originalText: The no‑arbitrage price is invariant to investor risk preferences
